# Recipe sheet: 21A American IPA, 20.0 L

## Style

**21A American IPA** (BJCP guide)

This beer is a decidedly hoppy and bitter, moderately strong, pale American ale. The balance is hop-forward with a clean fermentation profile and a dryish finish, allowing the creative range of hop character to shine through a clean, supporting malt base.

- Why this style: Picked 21A American IPA: the name matches (1.00).
  - Why: The recipe is identified as a 21A American IPA because the name matches the style definition perfectly. This style is characterized by a dominating hop balance in both aroma and flavor. [1]

## Targets and results

| Quantity | Target | Result | Style range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Batch (L) | 20.0 (stated) | 20.0 | – |
| Efficiency (%) | – | 72.0 | – |
| OG | 1.061 (derived) | 1.062 | 1.056–1.070 |
| FG | 1.011 (midpoint) | 1.012 | 1.008–1.014 |
| ABV (%) | 6.5 (stated) | 6.4 | 5.5–7.5 |
| IBU | 66.3 (hint) | 66.8 | 40–70 |
| SRM | 10.0 (midpoint) | 8.3 | 6–14 |

## Fermentables

- 5.10 kg Pale Ale Malt, 89.5 %
  - Why: Pale Ale Malt provides the clean, pale base malt foundation characteristic of American IPAs. It is the typical base malt used in this style to ensure the hop flavors are unimpeded. [2, 3]
- 0.30 kg Caramel 30 Malt, 5.3 %
  - Why: Caramel 30 Malt adds restrained caramel sweetness and light copper colour to support the hop profile. This level of caramel malt is typical for adding aroma and body without becoming cloying. [4]
- 0.30 kg Caramel 50 Malt, 5.3 %
  - Why: Caramel 50 Malt contributes deeper caramel notes and body to round out the malt character. It is a typical addition in this style to provide complexity alongside the base malt. [4]

## Hops

- 37 g Columbus, boil 60 min
  - Why: Columbus delivers the high bitterness required for the style with a spicy, lemony backbone. Boiling hops for 60 minutes is the standard method to isomerize alpha acids for maximum bitterness. [5]
- 28 g Citra, whirlpool 0 min
  - Why: Citra adds intense citrus and tropical aroma during the whirlpool phase. Whirlpool hopping is a common technique in American IPAs to preserve essential oils while allowing some isomerization. [6]
- 28 g Mosaic, dry hop 0 min
  - Why: Mosaic provides complex berry and pine aromas in the dry hop to finish the beer. Dry hopping is the best way to get fresh hop aroma into an IPA, and Mosaic is a typical variety for this purpose. [7]

## Yeast

- 23 g SafAle US-05
  - Pitch: 0.75 billion cells/L/degP (HTB ch. 7 p. 111-113) x 20 L x 15.1 degP = 226.5 billion cells; dry yeast at 10 billion cells per gram is HTB's generic figure (p. 108), not the maker's spec, so the 23 g are an estimate
  - Why: SafAle US-05 is a clean American ale yeast that ferments within the target attenuation band. It is a low ester, neutral-tasting yeast that allows the hop character to dominate, which is essential for this style. [8]

## Extras

- none

## How the amounts were worked out

- Colour: each fermentable counts at the middle of its EBC range: Pale Ale Malt 6.5, Caramel 30 Malt 30, Caramel 50 Malt 50
- Alpha: each hop counts at the middle of its alpha acid range: Columbus 16 %, Citra 12.5 %, Mosaic 12.5 %
- Attenuation: SafAle US-05 attenuates 80 %: the middle of its range [78,82] at a mash of 66.5 C (app.mash_attenuation)
- Fermentation temperature: 18 C, the temperature of the chosen "ferment at 18 °C"
- Boil: 60 min: the minimum boil time (rule 13)
- Mash: 66.5 C stays: the predicted FG 1.0123 is inside the range 1.0090 to 1.0130
- Colour moves: Pale Ale Malt is the darkest fermentable and no other base malt can take up the change
- Gravity: ABV 6.33 at OG 1.0613 is within 0.2 of the target 6.5, so the OG stays
- Rounding: Malts and flaked grains are weighed in 50 g steps, sugars in 1 g steps. Hops are weighed to the gram, at least 1 g.
- Yeast amount (SafAle US-05): 0.75 billion cells/L/degP (HTB ch. 7 p. 111-113) x 20 L x 15.1 degP = 226.5 billion cells; dry yeast at 10 billion cells per gram is HTB's generic figure (p. 108), not the maker's spec, so the 23 g are an estimate

## Water

- Why: The water profile targets an ale-medium-pale-assertive character with a mash pH of 5.336. This pH range is ideal for pale beers to ensure a refined bitterness and allow the singular malt character to shine. [9]
- Target: row ale-medium-pale-assertive, from style, basis listed (p. 122-123)
- Aim (mg/L): calcium 50, sulfate 363, chloride 13
- Salts:
  - gypsum 20.6 g (strike 11.1 g, sparge 9.5 g)
  - calcium chloride 0.8 g (strike 0.4 g, sparge 0.4 g)
- Mash pH: 5.34 (estimate, unverified against Bru'n Water); target 5.2–5.4
- Acid: no acid needed: the mash pH estimate 5.34 is not above 5.4 (target 5.2-5.4)

- Note: outside_row: alkalinity 0.0 mg/L as CaCO3 is below the row's [40,120] (a reference, not corrected)
- Note: outside_row: residual alkalinity -112.5 mg/L as CaCO3 is below the row's [-30,30] (a reference, not corrected)

## Mash

- Why: The mash schedule uses a single temperature infusion with a saccharification rest at 66.5 °C for 60 minutes. This is a simple and effective method for most beer styles, including American IPAs. [10]
- Strike water: 17.1 L at 72.7 °C (grain at 21.0 °C, 3.0 L/kg)
- Steps:
  - saccharification rest: 66.5 °C for 60 min
  - mash-out: 77.0 °C for 10 min
- Sparge water: 14.6 L (pre-boil volume 26.0 L)

## Boil

- Why: The boil time is 60 minutes, which is the minimum required to fully isomerize the alpha acids from the bittering hops. This ensures the beer reaches the target bitterness level. [5]
- Boil time: 60 min
- Because: 60 min: the minimum boil time (rule 13)
- 37 g Columbus, boil 60 min
- 28 g Citra, whirlpool 0 min

## Fermentation

- Why: The fermentation schedule includes a rest at 22 °C for 4 days, which helps with maturation and conditioning. The dry hop is added at 14 °C for 3 days, followed by a crash at 11 °C for 7 days to clarify the beer. [11]
- Steps:
  - ferment: 18.0 °C for 1 day
  - ferment: 19.0 °C for 2 days; move on: at least 2 more days (about day 3 of 4); move on to the rest when gravity within 2-5 points of FG (HTB p. 93-94, Table 6.2)
  - rest: 22.0 °C for 4 days; move on: starts when gravity within 2-5 points of FG (HTB p. 93-94, Table 6.2); stay at least 4 days (up to 8), then cool
  - dry_hop: 14.0 °C for 3 days
  - crash: 11.0 °C for 7 days
- Dry hops on day 7 at 14.0 °C, 3 days of contact: 28 g Mosaic

## Packaging

- Why: The packaging uses 117 g of table sugar to achieve a carbonation level of 2.45 volumes. This is a typical carbonation level for American ales, providing a crisp and assertive finish. [12]
- CO₂: 2.45 volumes; family american-ales, from style, basis inferred; range 2.2–2.7
- Priming: 117 g table sugar (sucrose) for 20.0 L, beer at 22.0 °C (5.9 g/L)

## Deviations

No deviations.

## Absent and unused items

None.

## Notes

- The dry hop contact time of 3 days at 14 °C is within the recommended range for IPAs to maximize aroma while minimizing grassy flavors. [7]
- The priming sugar amount is calculated to achieve a carbonation level of 2.45 volumes, which is typical for American ales. [12]

# Recipe sheet: 16B Oatmeal Stout, 20.0 L

## Style

**16B Oatmeal Stout** (BJCP guide)

This is a dark, roasty, and full-bodied stout with enough sweetness to support the oat backbone. The beer features a smooth, silky mouthfeel from the oats, balanced by deep chocolate and coffee roast flavors. It is a classic English-style oatmeal stout with a moderate alcohol content and a refined bitterness.

- Why this style: Picked 16B Oatmeal Stout: the name matches (1.00).
  - Why: The 16B Oatmeal Stout style was selected because the recipe name matches the style perfectly. This style is defined by the use of highly roasted malts and the smooth silkiness of oatmeal. [1]

## Targets and results

| Quantity | Target | Result | Style range |

| Batch (L) | 20.0 (profile) | 20.0 | – |
| Efficiency (%) | – | 72.0 | – |
| OG | 1.055 (midpoint) | 1.055 | 1.045–1.065 |
| FG | 1.014 (midpoint) | 1.013 | 1.010–1.018 |
| ABV (%) | 5.3 (derived) | 5.5 | 4.2–5.9 |
| IBU | 32.5 (midpoint) | 32.7 | 25–40 |
| SRM | 31.0 (midpoint) | 32.1 | 22–40 |

## Fermentables

- 3.70 kg Finest Pale Ale Maris Otter, 71.2 %
  - Why: Finest Pale Ale Maris Otter provides the clean, malty base and fermentable sugars necessary for the stout. It is an allowed base malt in this style that supports the overall structure. [2]
- 0.75 kg Flaked Oats, 14.4 %
  - Why: Flaked Oats are a typical ingredient in this style, adding the characteristic silky body and smooth mouthfeel. They are essential for defining the oatmeal stout profile. [1]
- 0.40 kg Caramel 150 Malt, 7.7 %
  - Why: Caramel 150 Malt is allowed in this style and contributes deep caramel and toffee notes. These flavors help balance the roast character of the darker malts. [1]
- 0.30 kg Chocolate Dark Malt, 5.8 %
  - Why: Chocolate Dark Malt is typical for stouts and delivers classic dark chocolate and coffee roast flavors. It contributes a deep ruby-black color and a pleasant roast character. [3]
- 0.05 kg Roasted Barley, 1.0 %
  - Why: Roasted Barley is typical in stouts and adds a dry, roasted grain character. It also deepens the color of the beer, contributing to the dark appearance. [4]

## Hops

- 50 g East Kent Golding, boil 60 min
  - Why: East Kent Golding is an allowed hop variety that provides the necessary bitterness with a subtle, traditional English floral character. This fits the style's requirement for a balanced, non-dominant hop profile. [5]

## Yeast

- 21 g SafAle S-04
  - Pitch: 0.75 billion cells/L/degP (HTB ch. 7 p. 111-113) x 20 L x 13.5 degP = 202.4 billion cells; dry yeast at 10 billion cells per gram is HTB's generic figure (p. 108), not the maker's spec, so the 21 g are an estimate
  - Why: SafAle S-04 is a typical English ale yeast that ferments cleanly and reaches the target attenuation. It is well-suited for styles with a balanced or light fermentation character. [6]

## Extras

- none

## How the amounts were worked out

- Colour: each fermentable counts at the middle of its EBC range: Finest Pale Ale Maris Otter 5.5, Flaked Oats 1.6, Caramel 150 Malt 150, Chocolate Dark Malt 900, Roasted Barley 1050

- Attenuation: SafAle S-04 attenuates 77.2 %: the middle of its range [74,82] at a mash of 68.5 C (app.mash_attenuation)
- Fermentation temperature: 15 C, the temperature of the chosen "ferment at 15 °C"
- Boil: 60 min: the minimum boil time (rule 13)
- Mash: 68.5 C stays: the brief hints at this mash temperature (predicted FG 1.0126, range 1.0100 to 1.0180)
- Colour moves: Roasted Barley 0.96 % to 0.51 %, Finest Pale Ale Maris Otter 70.58 % to 71.03 %: SRM 32.4 to 31.0 (target 31)
- Gravity: ABV 5.47 at OG 1.055 is within 0.2 of the target 5.27, so the OG stays

## Water

- Why: The water profile targets a medium-brown-black style with salts adjusted to achieve a mash pH of 5.402. This pH is within the recommended range for darker styles, preventing the need for acid additions. [7]

- Why: The mash schedule uses a strike temperature of 74.9 C and a saccharification rest at 68.5 C for 60 minutes. This single-rest approach is suitable for modern well-modified malts to achieve high yield and fermentability. [8]
- Strike water: 15.6 L at 74.9 °C (grain at 21.0 °C, 3.0 L/kg)
- Steps:

  - mash-out: 77.0 °C for 10 min

## Boil

- Why: The boil lasts 60 minutes, which is the minimum time required to ensure sufficient isomerization of alpha acids for bitterness. This duration allows the hops to contribute the intended IBU level. [9]
- Boil time: 60 min
- Because: 60 min: the minimum boil time (rule 13)
- 50 g East Kent Golding, boil 60 min

## Fermentation

- Why: The fermentation schedule starts at 15 C and ramps up to 19 C for a rest, followed by a crash to 8 C. This temperature management helps control byproduct formation and ensures a clean finish. [10]
- Steps:
  - ferment: 15.0 °C for 1 day
  - ferment: 16.0 °C for 2 days; move on: at least 2 more days (about day 3 of 4); move on to the rest when gravity within 2-5 points of FG (HTB p. 93-94, Table 6.2)

  - crash: 8.0 °C for 7 days

## Packaging

- Why: The beer is packaged with 2 volumes of CO2, which is typical for porters and stouts. Priming with table sugar ensures consistent carbonation without altering the flavor profile. [11]
- CO₂: 2.00 volumes; family porter-stout, from style, basis listed; range 1.7–2.3
- Priming: 82 g table sugar (sucrose) for 20.0 L, beer at 19.0 °C (4.1 g/L)

## Deviations

No deviations.

## Absent and unused items

None.

## Notes

- The mash-out step is included to help prevent a stuck sparge, which is a common risk when mashing with a significant proportion of flaked oats. [12]
- The water profile uses gypsum and calcium chloride to adjust the mash pH to the higher range recommended for darker styles, ensuring the malt character shines without one malt dominating. [7]
- Table sugar is used for priming because it is a simple sugar that carbonates the beer without adding significant flavor, which is suitable for a stout. [11]

**1B American Lager** (BJCP guide)

A very pale, highly-carbonated, light-bodied, and well-attenuated lager with a very neutral flavor profile and low bitterness. Served very cold, it is a refreshing and thirst-quenching drink.

## Style

**1C Cream Ale** (BJCP guide)

A clean, well-attenuated, and highly carbonated American "lawnmower" beer. It is easily drinkable, smooth, and refreshing, with more character than typical American lagers yet still subtle and restrained.

# Recipe sheet: 18B American Pale Ale, 20.0 L

## Style

**18B American Pale Ale** (BJCP guide)

An average-strength, hop-forward, pale American craft beer with sufficient supporting malt to make the beer balanced and drinkable. The clean hop presence can reflect classic or modern American or New World hop varieties with a wide range of characteristics.

- Why this style: Picked 18B American Pale Ale: the name matches (1.00).
  - Why: This recipe targets the 18B American Pale Ale style, which is defined by its hop-forward character and clean malt backbone. The name match confirms the stylistic intent for this batch. [1]

## Targets and results

| Quantity | Target | Result | Style range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Batch (L) | 20.0 (profile) | 20.0 | – |
| Efficiency (%) | – | 72.0 | – |
| OG | 1.053 (midpoint) | 1.051 | 1.045–1.060 |
| FG | 1.013 (midpoint) | 1.010 | 1.010–1.015 |
| ABV (%) | 5.2 (derived) | 5.3 | 4.5–6.2 |
| IBU | 40.0 (midpoint) | 39.9 | 30–50 |
| SRM | 7.5 (midpoint) | 6.1 | 5–10 |

## Fermentables

- 3.25 kg Pale Ale Malt, 69.9 %
  - Why: Pale Ale Malt provides the neutral, clean malt backbone characteristic of American Pale Ales. It is a typical base malt for this style, offering a warmer, toastier flavor than standard pale malt. [2]
- 0.95 kg Flaked Rice, 20.4 %
  - Why: Flaked Rice lightens the body and adds a crisp, dry finish to the beer. While out of style for traditional 18B recipes, it was included here to meet the request for rice. [3]
- 0.45 kg Caramel 30 Malt, 9.7 %
  - Why: Caramel 30 Malt adds subtle caramel notes and a touch of color to support the amber hue. It is a typical specialty malt addition for this style, providing roundness without overwhelming the hops. [4]

## Hops

- 31 g Centennial, boil 60 min
  - Why: Centennial delivers the primary bitterness and earthy-citrus backbone for the style. It is an allowed hop variety for American Pale Ales, often used as a substitute for or alongside Cascade. [5]
- 16 g Cascade, boil 0 min
  - Why: Cascade contributes classic grapefruit and floral aromas during the late boil. It is a typical hop choice for this style, providing the signature American hop character. [5]
- 16 g Cascade, dry hop 0 min

## Yeast

- 19 g SafAle US-05
  - Pitch: 0.75 billion cells/L/degP (HTB ch. 7 p. 111-113) x 20 L x 12.6 degP = 188.3 billion cells; dry yeast at 10 billion cells per gram is HTB's generic figure (p. 108), not the maker's spec, so the 19 g are an estimate
  - Why: SafAle US-05 is a clean American ale yeast that ferments to the target attenuation with minimal off-flavors. It is an allowed yeast for this style, producing a low-ester profile that lets the hops shine. [6]

## Extras

- none

## How the amounts were worked out

- Colour: each fermentable counts at the middle of its EBC range: Pale Ale Malt 6.5, Flaked Rice 2, Caramel 30 Malt 30
- Alpha: each hop counts at the middle of its alpha acid range: Centennial 10.5 %, Cascade 6.7 %, Cascade 6.7 %
- Attenuation: SafAle US-05 attenuates 80 %: the middle of its range [78,82] at a mash of 64.5 C (app.mash_attenuation)
- Fermentation temperature: 18 C, the temperature of the chosen "ferment at 18 °C"
- Boil: 60 min: the minimum boil time (rule 13)
- Mash: 64.5 C stays: the brief hints at this mash temperature (predicted FG 1.0101, range 1.0100 to 1.0150)
- Colour moves: Pale Ale Malt is the darkest fermentable and no other base malt can take up the change
- Gravity: ABV 5.42 at OG 1.0525 misses the target 5.15 by more than 0.2; OG moved to 1.0505 (at most 0.002) to give ABV 5.21
- Rounding: Malts and flaked grains are weighed in 50 g steps, sugars in 1 g steps; Flaked Rice is rounded away from the nearest step to keep the numbers and rules the exact amounts met. Hops are weighed to the gram, at least 1 g.
- Yeast amount (SafAle US-05): 0.75 billion cells/L/degP (HTB ch. 7 p. 111-113) x 20 L x 12.6 degP = 188.3 billion cells; dry yeast at 10 billion cells per gram is HTB's generic figure (p. 108), not the maker's spec, so the 19 g are an estimate

## Water

- Why: The water profile targets an ale-medium-pale-assertive character with gypsum and calcium chloride salts. The estimated mash pH of 5.35 is within the target range of 5.2-5.4, so no acid addition is needed. [7]
- Target: row ale-medium-pale-assertive, from style, basis listed (p. 122-123)
- Aim (mg/L): calcium 50, sulfate 363, chloride 13
- Salts:
  - gypsum 20.0 g (strike 9.1 g, sparge 10.9 g)
  - calcium chloride 0.8 g (strike 0.4 g, sparge 0.4 g)
- Mash pH: 5.35 (estimate, unverified against Bru'n Water); target 5.2–5.4
- Acid: no acid needed: the mash pH estimate 5.35 is not above 5.4 (target 5.2-5.4)
- Note: outside_row: calcium 159.7 mg/L is above the row's [50,150] (a reference, not corrected)
- Note: outside_row: alkalinity 0.0 mg/L as CaCO3 is below the row's [40,120] (a reference, not corrected)
- Note: outside_row: residual alkalinity -114.1 mg/L as CaCO3 is below the row's [-30,30] (a reference, not corrected)

## Mash

- Why: The mash schedule includes a beta-glucan rest and a saccharification rest at 64.5 C for 60 minutes. This multi-rest approach helps ensure full conversion and appropriate fermentability for the grain bill. [8]
- Strike water: 14.0 L at 48.2 °C (grain at 21.0 °C, 3.0 L/kg)
- Steps:
  - beta-glucan rest: 45.0 °C for 20 min
  - saccharification rest: 64.5 °C for 60 min
  - mash-out: 77.0 °C for 10 min
- Sparge water: 16.7 L (pre-boil volume 26.0 L)

## Boil

- Why: The 60-minute boil is the minimum time required to ensure sufficient isomerization of alpha acids for bitterness. This duration allows for the proper extraction of hop resins while preserving aroma oils from late additions. [9]
- Boil time: 60 min
- Because: 60 min: the minimum boil time (rule 13)
- 31 g Centennial, boil 60 min
- 16 g Cascade, boil 0 min

## Fermentation

- Why: The fermentation schedule ramps from 18 C to 22 C, which is within the suggested range for American ale yeasts. The dry hop at 14 C and crash at 11 C help clarify the beer and settle the yeast. [6]
- Steps:
  - ferment: 18.0 °C for 1 day
  - ferment: 19.0 °C for 2 days; move on: at least 2 more days (about day 3 of 4); move on to the rest when gravity within 2-5 points of FG (HTB p. 93-94, Table 6.2)
  - rest: 22.0 °C for 4 days; move on: starts when gravity within 2-5 points of FG (HTB p. 93-94, Table 6.2); stay at least 4 days (up to 8), then cool
  - dry_hop: 14.0 °C for 3 days
  - crash: 11.0 °C for 7 days
- Dry hops on day 7 at 14.0 °C, 3 days of contact: 16 g Cascade

## Packaging

- Why: The packaging targets 2.45 volumes of CO2, which is inferred for American ales. Priming with 117 g of table sugar is a standard method to achieve this carbonation level without adding significant flavor. [10]
- CO₂: 2.45 volumes; family american-ales, from style, basis inferred; range 2.2–2.7
- Priming: 117 g table sugar (sucrose) for 20.0 L, beer at 22.0 °C (5.9 g/L)

## Deviations

|---|---|---|---|---|
| rice | ingredient | out of style | you asked | Flaked Rice (mash) is the closest choice: not a usual ingredient of American Pale Ale (18B) |

## Absent and unused items

None.

## Notes

- Flaked rice must be mashed with the base malt to ensure proper starch conversion. [3]
- American pale ale is considered to have a very clean character, so it should be pitched at a higher rate of 1.0 billion cells per liter per 4 gravity points. [11]
- The priming sugar amount is consistent with producing about 2.5 volumes of CO2, which is typical for American pale ales. [10]

## Style

**mexican-style-amber-lager Mexican-Style Amber Lager** (BA guide)

This is a clean, dry amber lager with a warm malt character and a crisp finish. It balances caramel and toffee notes from specialty malts with a light body and moderate bitterness.

- Why this style: Picked mexican-style-amber-lager Mexican-Style Amber Lager: the name matches (1.00).
  - Why: This style is a New World variation of the Vienna lager, characterized by its amber color and clean lager profile. It suits brewers looking for a crisp, malty beer with a dry finish. [1]

- 0.90 kg Flaked Rice, 20.5 %
  - Why: Flaked Rice lightens the body and adds crispness, which is characteristic of Mexican-style lagers. It helps achieve the dry finish and lighter mouthfeel typical of the style. [3]

  - Why: Caraamber adds caramel and toffee notes that support the amber color and malt profile. It is a typical ingredient for this style, providing depth without excessive sweetness. [4]

  - Why: Diamond is a clean lager yeast that reaches the required attenuation band for a dry finish. It is well-suited for this style, producing a crisp and clean beer with low esters. [6]

- Pitch the lager yeast cold and ferment warm to ensure a clean fermentation and proper attenuation. [9]
